In [[functional analysis]], the '''Dunford–Pettis property''', named after [[Nelson Dunford]] and [[B. J. Pettis]], is a property of a [[Banach space]] stating that all weakly compact operators from this space into another Banach space are completely continuous. Many standard Banach spaces have this property, most notably, the space <math>C(K)</math> of continuous functions on a [[compact space]] and the space [[Lp space|<math>L^1(\mu)</math>]] of the Lebesgue integrable functions on a [[measure space]]. [[Alexander Grothendieck]] introduced the concept in the early 1950s {{harv|Grothendieck|1953}}, following the work of [[Dunford]] and Pettis, who developed earlier results of [[Shizuo Kakutani]], [[Kōsaku Yosida]], and several others. Important results were obtained more recently by [[Jean Bourgain]]. Nevertheless, the Dunford–Pettis property is not completely understood.

==Definition==

A Banach space <math>X</math> has the '''Dunford–Pettis property''' if every continuous weakly [[compact operator]] <math display="inline">T : X \to Y</math> from <math>X</math> into another Banach space <math>Y</math>  transforms weakly compact sets in <math>X</math> into norm-compact sets in <math>Y</math> (such operators are called [[completely continuous]]). An important equivalent definition is that for any [[weak topology|weakly convergent]] [[sequence (mathematics)|sequence]]s <math>x_1, x_2, \ldots</math> of <math>X</math> and <math>f_1, f_2, \ldots</math> of the [[dual space]] <math>X^*,</math> converging (weakly) to <math>x</math> and <math>f,</math> the sequence <math>f_1(x_1), f_2(x_2), \ldots, f_n(x_n), \ldots</math> converges to <math>f(x).</math>

==Counterexamples==

* The second definition may appear counterintuitive at first, but consider an orthonormal basis <math>e_n</math> of an infinite-dimensional, separable Hilbert space <math>H.</math> Then <math>e_n \to 0</math> weakly, but for all <math>n</math> <math display=block>\langle e_n, e_n\rangle = 1.</math> Thus separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces cannot have the Dunford–Pettis property.
* Consider as another example the space <math>L^p(-\pi, \pi)</math> where <math display="inline">1 < p < \infty.</math>  The sequences <math>x_n = e^{inx}</math> in <math>L^p</math> and <math>f_n = e^{inx}</math> in <math>L^q = \left(L^p\right)^*</math> both converge weakly to zero.  But <math display=block>\langle f_n, x_n \rangle = \int\limits_{-\pi}^\pi 1\, {\rm d}x = 2 \pi.</math>
* More generally, no infinite-dimensional [[reflexive Banach space]] may have the Dunford–Pettis property. In particular, an infinite-dimensional [[Hilbert space]] and more generally, [[Lp space]]s with <math>1 < p < \infty</math> do not possess this property.

==Examples==

* If <math>K</math> is a [[compact Hausdorff space]], then the Banach space <math>C(K)</math> of [[continuous function]]s with the [[uniform norm]] has the Dunford–Pettis property.
